title: Dead faith is still God's gift and true in itself; the wicked assent inwardly but use faith badly
source_text: VIII. Caeterum docent Scholae Romanae Theologi illum qui fidem solum mortuam & informem habet, non bene credere, neque sicut oportet, ut videre est apud Bellarminum, lib. 1. de Justificatione, pluribus in locis. Sed pertendent nihilominus illam esse Dei donum, & ad gratiam pertinere, & titulum ac nomen verae fidei mereri. Nempe, ex ipsorum mente, assensus ille quem praebent verbo Dei multi mali Christiani, in se quidem bonus est, & a Deo inspiratus, ac per eum intus & reipsa, non externe tantum atque simulate, assentiuntur doctrinae divinae atque verissimae, male tamen credunt & non sicut oportet, quia fide sua non recte utuntur, nec ad debitum finem illam referunt, neque faciunt illa quae fides facienda dictat. Hoc est quod docet Stapletonus. Etsi, inquit, actus fidei sine charitate bonus est, tamen non bene fit, adeoque post bonus non est. Ideo autem non bene fit, quia ad finem boni ultimum talis actus non dirigitur. De Justif. lib. 8. cap. 9.
pass_a_gloss: But the Theologians of the Roman School teach that he who has only dead and unformed faith does not believe well, nor as he ought, as may be seen in Bellarmine, book 1 on Justification, in several places. Yet they nevertheless contend that it is a gift of God, and pertains to grace, and deserves the title and name of true faith. Namely, on their mind, that assent which many bad Christians give to the word of God is in itself indeed good and inspired by God, and through it they inwardly and in reality, not only outwardly and by pretense, assent to the divine and most true doctrine; yet they believe badly and not as they ought, because they do not use their faith rightly, nor refer it to the due end, nor do those things which faith dictates to be done. This is what Stapleton teaches. Although, he says, the act of faith without charity is good, yet it is not done well, and so afterward it is not good. But therefore it is not done well, because such an act is not directed to the ultimate end of the good. On Justification, book 8, chapter 9.
pass_b_english: Rome still calls dead, unformed faith a divine gift that merits the name of true faith — even while saying its holders do not believe well or as they ought.
Bad Christians' assent to the Word is inwardly real and God-inspired, yet they misuse faith, miss its due end, and omit what faith commands.
Stapleton: the act without charity is good in itself, but not well done because it is not aimed at the ultimate good.
